seal.statement: Every production semantic interaction in the measured formation proof cone has exactly one authoritative formation owner at its semantic boundary, or is explicitly demonstrated to be outside the semantic-attribution domain. No generic execution mechanism - the execution-node context, VirtualNetwork delivery, a promise continuation, a remote peer representation, the transcript or observer machinery - may become a semantic owner, and no owner may be supplied by a fallback or default. Until that is established, neither the per-owner totals nor the unattributed fraction is admissible evidence about anything.

text:
F0: THE RED CONTROL WAS NOT STALE. IT WAS RUNNER-DEPENDENT, AND IT PROVED LESS
THAN ITS ASSERTIONS CLAIMED.

The inventory first, because the mutation's authority depends on it. Two
functions carry the whole Raft interaction contract, and exactly three
production modules consume them:

  runRaftProtocolActivity   liferaft-timing-api.js      2 sites
                              heartbeatWithEndGuard -> super.heartbeat
                              indefinitelyWithProtocolAttribution
                            liferaft-incoming-data.js   1 site
                              the DATA dispatch at the inbound boundary
  runRaftApplySlice         liferaft-commit-scheduler.js 1 site
                              the commit/apply turn

liferaft.js itself does NOT import the interaction module. It imports those
three. That matters, because the mutation was injected as
t.mockImport(liferaft.js, {interaction: mutatedModule}) - a specifier
liferaft.js never names.

WHY THE VERDICT FLIPPED. The file is a tap test. Under `node scripts/
run-test-files.js` (the project's runner) and under `npx tap` it was green:
42 of 42. Under `node --test` or plain `node` it was red with five assertion
failures. That is not two views of one defect; it is two different programs.
t.mockImport needs tap's loader, and without it the call silently returns the
REAL module: the mutation never happens, the reverted arm behaves exactly like
the current one, and assertions demanding zero see the full unmutated duration.
Measured directly: with a recorder substituted for the interaction module, the
recorder observed zero calls under plain node, at any depth - even mocking a
direct dependency of liferaft.js. So the earlier report that the simulation and
raft suites carried one pre-existing red was an artifact of running a tap file
under node --test. Corrected: under the project's runner that file was green
before E and is green now.

WHAT THE CONTROL ACTUALLY PROVED, EVEN WHEN IT RAN. Two weaknesses survived the
runner question.

First, nothing verified that the mutated module was the instance production
resolved. The four `expected 0` assertions would also pass if the scenario had
silently executed no production work at all - a mutation that suppresses rather
than severs. The instruction not to trust source-string replacement plus one
mocked specifier by inspection was exactly right: inspection would have said the
mock was inert, and inspection would have been wrong in the other direction
under tap.

Second, `raft_protocol duration must equal exactly 0` is an accounting claim,
not a semantic one. It says a bucket is empty. It does not say that an
ownership TRANSITION failed to occur, and it cannot distinguish "the boundary
was not crossed" from "no work ran".

THE REPAIR, in three parts.

1. The consumer inventory is now asserted, not inspected. The witness walks
   src/ and requires the set of modules importing the interaction contract to
   be exactly those three. A fourth consumer would be exercised by the host
   while sitting outside the mutation; now it turns the witness red instead.

2. Every loaded variant is instrumented and records WHICH production module
   entered it, taken from the call stack at entry. The witness then asserts
   coverage per exercised path: heartbeat and indefinite retry enter from
   liferaft-timing-api.js, inbound DATA from liferaft-incoming-data.js, the
   commit turn from liferaft-commit-scheduler.js. An empty record now fails
   first, and says so in one sentence, instead of producing five confusing
   numeric mismatches. Running the repaired witness under plain node now
   reports 'production resolved the mutated interaction module: an empty
   record means the substitution never applied' rather than 'expected 0,
   got 10'.

   That instrument also produced an observation worth keeping: the apply run
   enters protocol from BOTH incoming-data and timing-api, because the LifeRaft
   constructor arms its heartbeat through the timing API. Construction is a
   protocol entry.

3. The falsifier is now semantic. From a neutral parent - the accounting
   owner's own `unattributed`, since normalizeOwner maps an empty store to it -
   the witness samples the owner in force INSIDE the production callback, by
   the accounting owner's own rule (the active segment while JavaScript runs,
   the async-local store otherwise):

     current mapping   every sampled owner is raft_protocol
     reverted mapping  the same number of production callbacks still execute
                       and every sampled owner is still unattributed

   The claim is the transition, and the equal sample count is what rules out
   'the work simply did not run'. For apply the nested distinction is kept
   whole: parent raft_protocol in both arms; under the current mapping the
   apply turn is raft_apply with handoffCount 1 - a new semantic boundary, not
   an inherited dispatch - and under the revert the apply work stays under the
   parent protocol owner with raft_apply receiving no duration and no handoff.

   Inactive behaviour equality is retained unchanged.

The witness is green under the project runner at 73 assertions, and its failure
under a runner without the mock loader is now a diagnosis rather than a puzzle.

F1: THE ATTRIBUTION SEMANTICS ARE SEALED, AND SEALING THEM CHANGED WHAT THE
CENSUS IS ALLOWED TO INFER.

WHO MAY ASSIGN A SEMANTIC OWNER, AND WHERE. Two modules, and only two, call
runFormationOwner:

  formation-owner-attribution.js   7 entries: admin, bootstrap,
                                   membership_publication, readiness,
                                   rebalancer, transport, worker_dispatch
  raft-formation-attribution.js    2 entries: raft_protocol, raft_apply

Fourteen production modules consume them - eleven the general entries, three
the Raft ones. That is the complete assignment surface. Nothing else in src/
can name an owner, and the F0 witness now asserts the Raft half of that
inventory rather than inspecting it.

THE FOUR CASES, each established on real objects rather than a synthetic hook
harness, 40 assertions green.

  Direct entry. An unowned execution that crosses runBootstrapActivity is
  bootstrap INSIDE and unattributed on both sides; bootstrap is charged the
  enclosed work and nothing around it.

  Async inheritance. Work armed inside an owner runs as that owner across a
  real timer, and a second generation armed from the first keeps it with no
  further wrapper.

  Explicit handoff. A nested entry is exclusively the callee, the caller
  resumes after it returns, the callee is charged exactly its own region, and
  the two are never simultaneously authoritative.

  Neutral carrier. Five generic mechanisms carry execution without inventing
  an owner: runOnExecutionNode, a microtask continuation, VirtualNetwork timer
  delivery, a remote peer representation (both write and end), and the host
  transcript. With only carriers exercised, busy duration is zero and the
  unattributed bucket is zero as well - nothing was laundered.

  Both production falsifiers hold on real objects. A bootstrap parent that
  calls raft.heartbeat() arms its timer as raft_protocol and is restored to
  bootstrap afterwards; a transport-inbound parent that emits a real DATA
  packet has the dispatch execute as raft_protocol and is restored to
  transport. Neither owns Raft because it made the call. Overlap and partition
  delta are zero in both.

TWO PROPERTIES OF THE ACCOUNTING OWNER THAT THE CENSUS MUST NOT ASSUME AWAY.
Both were found by an assertion failing, not by reading the source, and both
change F2's design.

  1. IDLE IS NOT UNATTRIBUTED. Time when no segment is running is idle wall
     time. `unattributed` is reserved for a DISPATCHED turn that carried no
     owner. These are different populations and the census must not merge
     them: a residual measured as "unattributed" is a statement about turns,
     not about wall time.

  2. AN EXPLICIT ENTRY FROM A NEUTRAL PARENT IS IN NEITHER COUNTER.
     runFormationOwner never counts a dispatch, and counts a handoff only when
     another owner is already active. So:

       neutral parent -> runFormationOwner(X)   counted nowhere
       owner A active -> runFormationOwner(B)   handoffCount[B] += 1
       async resource dispatched                dispatchCount[owner] += 1

     Measured directly: an explicit bootstrap entry that then armed two timer
     generations produced handoffCount 0 and dispatchCount 2 - the two
     inherited generations only. The lineage's own starting point is invisible.

     This is exactly the distinction F2 is required to preserve, so F2 cannot
     recover it from the snapshot. The census must OBSERVE the entry itself.
     That is observation added alongside owner assignment, not a change to it:
     the counters stay as they are, because changing them would change what
     every existing owner proof means.

F2/F3: THE PROVENANCE CENSUS OVER THE COMPLETE E HOST, AND WHY F STOPS HERE.

METHOD. An attribution window is opened around the exact E chain
(runSeedHandoffScenario: 138 owner runtimes, 276 peer representations,
production peer writes, normal teardown; strict reports violations=0
substitutions=0 eligible=true ledger=0). Observation only: a wrapping
hookFactory records, per async resource, its creation frame and its trigger
parent, and FormationTurnAttribution.prototype.run is wrapped to see every
explicit entry and handoff. No owner assignment is altered to obtain the
reading; the wrapper delegates to the real implementation in every case.

Provenance is taken from the creation frame, and where a frameless promise has
none, from the nearest framed ancestor in its trigger chain. Where that also
fails, from the first resource the segment itself creates while running - what
the code DID, when where it came from is unavailable.

THE POPULATION. 744,710 dispatched segments.

  558,542  async descendant of an authoritative owner
  186,168  no owner at dispatch
             5,975 of them entered an owner boundary during the segment
           180,193 never entered one

EXPLICIT OWNER ENTRY IS ALMOST ABSENT. Every runFormationOwner call in the
whole chain, by owner and kind:

  raft_protocol   46,937 handoffs,  30 entries
  raft_apply       3,101 handoffs,   0 entries
  transport            1 handoff,    0 entries
  admin, bootstrap, membership_publication, readiness, rebalancer,
  worker_dispatch                    0

Three of nine owners are exercised at all, and one of those exactly once. The
earlier remeasure recorded six buckets at zero; this says WHY. It is not that
those owners did no work. It is that their entry points are not on this path.

WHERE THE UNATTRIBUTED WORK COMES FROM. By the module that created it
(count, and inclusive wall time - inclusive, because a parent segment's time
contains its children's, so these are not a partition and must not be summed
against the window):

    55,684   1461.6 ms  src/raft
    11,669   1313.5 ms  src/bootstrap
     8,844   1298.3 ms  frameless, and unresolved
    11,079   1116.1 ms  src/cdc
     5,176    655.8 ms  test/simulation
    17,054    490.0 ms  src/partition
     4,657    293.8 ms  src/service
    33,029    256.9 ms  src/transport
     4,560    150.5 ms  src/topology
     3,736    103.4 ms  src/control-plane
     7,359     60.6 ms  src/message-group
    23,077     22.6 ms  frameless and inert (creates nothing; ~1 us each)
       243      20.8 ms  src/query, src/config, src/runtime, src/node,
                         test/distributed

Harness-created work is 5,180 segments of 186,168 - 2.8 percent. Everything
else was created by production modules, and the modules concerned are mutation
and propagation owners: partition-service-raft-write-commit,
authoritative-row-mutation-helper, partition-service-row-owner,
cdc-integration-service-coalesced-mutation, partition-cdc-delivery,
cdc-group-propagation-service, the message-group CDC replication runtimes.
This work reaches effects - the run commits 549 raft log entries and hydrates
the system cache - so it is not inert plumbing.

CLASSIFICATION, and the three reasons F cannot proceed to repair.

  OUTSIDE_DOMAIN, provable: 23,077 frameless inert continuations, which create
  nothing and cost about a microsecond each - the resumption steps of an await
  whose awaiter is external, which the accounting owner already documents as
  deliberately unattributed. Plus, pending per-segment proof, the 5,180
  harness-created segments.

  UNKNOWN: 8,844 frameless segments that are NOT inert (1.3 s inclusive) and
  for which neither creation frame, ancestry, nor first nested creation yields
  a repository frame. That is 4.8 percent of the residual and it is materially
  non-zero. F3 says stop rather than call it harmless, so this alone is a stop.

  PRODUCTION_UNOWNED, and this is the finding that matters: roughly 148,000
  segments created by production modules, whose first missing semantic boundary
  is not missing by oversight. It does not exist, or it is not on this path.

    bootstrap  The boundary exists and is crossed in production:
               StartupPipelineRunner wraps every phase in
               runBootstrapActivity. The simulator enters production one level
               BELOW it, calling bootstrap.seedInfrastructurePhase
               .phaseInfrastructure() and its siblings directly - the
               composition authorised in A2b. So bootstrap work is unowned
               here because of where the cone enters, not because production
               forgot a boundary.

    transport  The boundary is handleMessage(), the PHYSICAL websocket frame
               handler. Exactly one physical frame crosses in this
               composition, which is the A2a fidelity decision, so the
               boundary is crossed once. The 16,334 peer writes and the whole
               in-process delivery path never reach it. Attributing them would
               mean moving the boundary from the physical frame handler to the
               delivery entry - a production ownership decision.

    partition, cdc, message-group, service lifecycle, topology,
    control-plane gateway
               There is NO boundary to cross. The owner vocabulary is admin,
               bootstrap, membership_publication, raft_apply, raft_protocol,
               readiness, rebalancer, transport, worker_dispatch. None of them
               owns partition-service work, CDC propagation or service
               lifecycle. A CDC continuation that resumes after an await has
               no semantic boundary available to it. It is unattributable by
               construction.

  Any attempt to give that last group an owner without first deciding the
  vocabulary would be exactly the catch-all the quest forbids: inheriting the
  execution node's owner, the previous owner, or the nearest enclosing one.

TWO MEASUREMENTS THAT ARE NOT COMPARABLE TO ANYTHING, recorded as definitions
rather than as results. By segment count, 25.0 percent of dispatches carry no
owner. By the accounting owner's own duration partition over this window,
unattributedPercent reads 65.2. These measure different things over a
different window from the ~34 percent figure, and per the quest constraint no
comparison is drawn between them. overlapDurationUs and partitionDeltaUs are
both 0 throughout.

F3a: OWNER-ENTRY REACHABILITY MATRIX. Nine owners, their real production
entries, and what the E chain does with each. No source changed to produce it.

Evidence per row: (i) every runFormationOwner call in the run, by owner and
kind; (ii) the creation site of every unattributed async resource; (iii) the
first resource each unattributed segment creates while running - what the code
was doing when where it came from is unavailable.

  OWNER                    CANONICAL PRODUCTION ENTRY                 E REACHES  SUBSYSTEM WORK  CLASS
  raft_protocol            liferaft-timing-api heartbeat/indefinite   yes        yes             REACHED
                           liferaft-incoming-data DATA dispatch       30 entries, 46,937 handoffs
  raft_apply               liferaft-commit-scheduler commit turn      yes        yes             REACHED
                                                                      3,101 handoffs
  transport                message-router-inbound-dispatch            yes        yes             REACHED, sparse
                             .handleMessage (REMOTE inbound)          1 handoff
  bootstrap                startup-pipeline-runner .run phases        NO         YES             BYPASSED
                             and .runWorkflow steps                   0 entries  all five phases
  admin                    admin-websocket-message-dispatch           no         no              NOT_EXERCISED
                           schema-provisioning-job-owner.executeJob   0 segments created or run
  rebalancer               unified-rebalancer-lifecycle reconcile     no         no              NOT_EXERCISED
                           operation-workflow-dispatch-execution      0 segments created or run
                           replica-dispatch-service-lifecycle
  membership_publication   membership-publication-coordinator-reads   no         no              NOT_EXERCISED
                           replica-dispatch publication advance       0 segments created or run
  readiness                readiness-planning-snapshot-owner          no         no              NOT_EXERCISED
                             .reconcile                               0 segments created or run
  worker_dispatch          replica-worker-manager executionPool.run   no         no              NOT_EXERCISED
                           replica-worker-manager-replica-creation    0 segments created or run

THE ONE BYPASSED ROW. StartupPipelineRunner wraps every phase in
runBootstrapActivity at .run() and every workflow step at .runWorkflow(). The
seed host calls bootstrap.seedInfrastructurePhase.phaseInfrastructure() and its
four siblings directly, one level below that boundary. The phases execute; the
owner entry does not. That is a correspondence defect and it is the only one
the matrix finds.

THE FIVE NOT_EXERCISED ROWS ARE LEGITIMATE ZEROS. admin, rebalancer and
worker_dispatch created and ran ZERO async resources in the whole run - not one
segment anywhere is rooted in src/admin, src/rebalancer or src/worker. E is a
cold seed that never joins a node, never rebalances and never dispatches to a
worker, so their subsystems do not run at all. The limit of this evidence,
stated rather than hidden: it observes async resource creation and execution,
so a purely synchronous path that creates nothing would escape it. For three
queue-driven subsystems that is not a plausible shape.

membership_publication and readiness need a sharper statement, because
src/control-plane DOES appear in the residual - 3,736 segments. Every one of
them is the SYSTEM TABLE GATEWAY:

    1,148  control-plane-system-table-gateway-read-dispatch.js
    1,056  control-plane-system-table-gateway-request-coalescing.js
    1,040  control-plane-system-table-gateway-mutation-submission.js
      328  control-plane-system-table-gateway-read-strategies.js
      164  control-plane-system-table-gateway-query-execution.js

None is membership-publication-coordinator-reads, readiness-planning-snapshot-
owner or replica-dispatch-service-lifecycle. The publication and readiness
owners are not running. The gateway is a shared read/write path entered BY
other owners' work, so it is an ownership-propagation question (F3c), not
evidence that either owner was bypassed.

CONCLUSION FOR F3a. One repair is authorised by the matrix and one only: route
the five seed phases through StartupPipelineRunner so the existing bootstrap
owner is entered. No other owner's boundary moves, and no owner is added.

F3b/F3c/F3d: THREE LINEAGE REPAIRS, AND A CORRECTION TO MY OWN CENSUS.

FIRST, THE CORRECTION, because it invalidates a number I reported. The 8,844
UNKNOWN segments with no repository frame were not a property of the system.
They were ES module loading. My census opened the attribution window and THEN
dynamically imported the production graph, so every promise-resolution step of
loading several hundred modules was counted as an unattributed dispatch. Load
the graph before the window opens and they are gone: 31,940 frameless segments
become 1. The earlier statement that UNKNOWN was materially non-zero was a
measurement defect of mine, not evidence about attribution. Every count below
is measured with the graph loaded outside the window.

THE THREE REPAIRS, each traced to its causal root before anything was changed.

  1. BOOTSTRAP, C1 - the cone entered below the boundary. The five seed phases
     now run through the real StartupPipelineRunner.run({phases: [...]}), one
     phase per call, exactly as the production seed workflow runs them. The
     harness declares no owner; it enters through the production module that
     already owns the interaction. The phase set is unchanged.

  2. THE PROTOCOL TASK TRACKER, C2 - owner entered, lineage dropped one
     statement later. liferaft-incoming-data patched the inbound DATA listener
     as

         const dispatched = runRaftProtocolActivity(() => dispatch(...));
         return raft.protocolTasks.track(dispatched);

     The tracker keeps its bookkeeping in promises of its own, and they were
     created AFTER the owner's region closed, so every continuation of the same
     inbound dispatch ran unowned. track() now happens inside the region. The
     boundary did not move; it is still the inbound DATA dispatch, and the
     caller still receives the base library's own task.

  3. THE VIRTUAL TIMER SUBSTRATE, a substrate-fidelity defect in the harness.
     A real setTimeout creates a Timeout async resource when the timer is ARMED
     and dispatches the callback inside it; that resource is how async context,
     and therefore the formation owner, reaches the callback. VirtualNetwork's
     adapter timer called record.fn(...) straight out of its drain loop, so
     every timer-fired Raft callback began with no owner - in a live process
     the same callback would have inherited raft_protocol. The adapter timer
     now carries an AsyncResource from arm to fire. It names no owner; it stops
     destroying the one the arming context had. This is the same rule the
     clock work established: determinism must substitute the substrate, not
     silently alter its semantics.

     This one repair resolved the entire transport and partition residual.
     They were never transport-owned work: they were outbound peer writes and
     partition raft-init continuations DOWNSTREAM of a timer-fired Raft
     callback, and once the callback was owned they inherited it. The inbound
     transport boundary was not moved and runTransportInboundActivity is
     exactly where it was.

    segments observed          744,710    717,130
    owned by inheritance       558,542    712,997
    unattributed               186,168      4,133
    unattributed, inclusive      76.2%       3.29%
    src/raft                    55,684          0
    src/transport               33,029          9
    src/partition               17,054        135

    src/message-group            7,359          6
    src/service                  4,657          0
    src/topology                 4,560          0
    src/control-plane            3,736          0

  Owner entries now recorded: raft_protocol 29 entries / 46,938 handoffs,
  raft_apply 3,101 handoffs, bootstrap 5 handoffs (one per seed phase),
  transport 1 handoff. Still three of nine owners, and the other six remain
  legitimately NOT_EXERCISED per the F3a matrix.

WHAT REMAINS, split by whether it happens while the formation forms or while
the scenario ends. The split is taken at the moment the production shutdown
owner is entered.

  FORMATION            3,516
    harness scheduling 3,510   formation-sim-quiescence 1,713,

    production             5   startup-pipeline-runner's own per-phase
                               continuation: it accumulates completedPhases
                               and calls emit() on an eventSink that is null
                               in this composition, so it mutates nothing and

                               continuation mechanics
    frameless              1

  TEARDOWN               617
    production           593   seed-cleanup-handler 428,

                               message-router-stats-shutdown 9,

                               runtime shutdown 3, misc 8
    harness               24

E IS UNCHANGED THROUGHOUT. ownerAddressCount 138, peerObjectCount 276,
peerAddressCount 138, runtimesInPeerSlots [], authorityBreaches [],
peer write 16,334, end 138, pending 0, strict violations=0 substitutions=0
eligible=true. The four artifacts are byte-identical to E's committed receipt
after all three repairs - tx 74904e435167e552, net ce093df170ac094f over 4,813
lines, prov bc6f3f2adb84db30, nowMs 4455 - measured twice.

RED ON REVERT. A new witness replaces StartupPipelineRunner with one that
invokes phase.run() itself. Mutation integrity is asserted first (the reverted
runner ran both phases), then: bootstrap entries 2 -> 0, while the same
message-group runtimes exist, the host transcript is identical, and strict and
pending are identical. The boundary matters for attribution and for nothing
else.

F3c/F3e FINAL CLASSIFICATION. Every remaining unattributed segment in the
formation cone is named by its creation site and classified by what the code at
that site does, never by which directory it lives in.

A second census artefact had to be corrected first, for the same reason as the
module-loading one. The deterministic owner guard wraps the global timer
functions, so ITS frame was the first repository frame at creation and it
masked whoever actually armed the timer. It is a transparent interceptor, like
the census's own hook, and is now seen through. 1,314 segments that looked like
guard work are the seed host's own turn.

FORMATION RESIDUAL, 3,516 segments, every site accounted for:

  1,314+6  seed host :334   const hostTurn = () =>
                            new Promise((resolve) => setImmediate(resolve))
                            One macrotask offered to the closure authority.
                            Creates a promise, resolves on setImmediate,
                            returns. Calls no production code.
  1,274+6  quiescence :238  for (const owner of owners) await owner();
                            The closure authority awaiting each owner-idle
                            contract; the continuation resumes its own loop.
    433    quiescence :264  await closeCurrentInstant(...) inside
                            advanceToNextInstant - the scheduler drive loop.
    384    seed host :401   await advanceToNextInstant(...) inside
                            driveUntilSettled - the same drive loop.
     ~90   seed host        the host's phase wrappers and scenario driver
                            awaits, same family.
      5    startup-pipeline-runner :95
      1    frameless

OUTSIDE_DOMAIN is claimed for the harness sites on the code at each site: they
create a promise or await one, and resume a loop. No semantic decision, no
production mutation, no production enqueue, no owner entry, no effect beyond
continuation mechanics. Every one of them is the scenario's scheduler, which is
the harness's own authority and never production's.

THE FIVE PRODUCTION SEGMENTS, and a small repair that makes their proof
unconditional. They were the continuation of

    await runBootstrapActivity(() => phase.run());
    completedPhases.push(phase.name);
    this.emit(PHASE_COMPLETE, {phase: phase.name});

so a phase's own completion record and notification ran OUTSIDE the owner that
ran the phase. Both now sit inside the region. What remains at the await is the
loop's next step and nothing else - and that is the one thing an entry boundary
structurally cannot put inside the owner it enters. Five segments, mechanical,
unconditionally outside the domain rather than outside-because-the-event-sink-
happened-to-be-null.

  Measured after: bootstrap 1 entry + 4 handoffs (five seed phases, the first
  from a synchronous parent and the rest from inside a dispatch), and the same
  5 boundary continuations remain at the await, now carrying nothing.

So for the formation cone: productionSemanticUnowned = 0, unknown = 1 (one
frameless segment), ambiguousSemanticOwner = 0, overlapDurationUs = 0,
partitionDeltaUs = 0, and no owner was added, no boundary moved outward into a
carrier, and no fallback exists.

E remains: 138 / 276 / 138, no runtime in a peer slot, no authority breach,
16,334 peer writes, zero pending, strict violations=0 substitutions=0
eligible=true, artifacts byte-identical to E's receipt. 272 test files green
(9,391 assertions) across simulation, raft, diagnostics and bootstrap; the
static gate is green with every ratchet at its baseline.

THE TEARDOWN RESIDUAL IS A SCOPE QUESTION, NOT AN ACCOUNTING ONE, and it is
where F stops. 593 production segments run after the production shutdown owner
is entered: seed-cleanup-handler 428, partition-service-lifecycle-methods 135,
message-router-stats-shutdown 9, message-group cache/lifecycle 6,
bootstrap-service-runtime-methods 5, runtime shutdown 3, misc 7. They do real
production work - they stop 135 replica runtimes - so they are not continuation
mechanics and cannot be called outside-domain on the stated criteria.

They are also not a composition bypass. In production, node shutdown is reached
from entrypoint-runtime-shutdown-lifecycle on a process signal, and nothing on
that path enters a formation owner either. StartupPipelineRunner says so
explicitly: cleanup is deliberately NOT the runner's, it belongs to
SeedCleanupHandler - a code owner with no formation-attribution entry.

So by the C1/C2/C3 test this is C3: effectful production work that none of the
nine owners semantically owns. Per the standing instruction that is a STOP and
not a tenth owner. But it turns on a scoping question the owner should settle
first, because the two readings give different answers and only one of them
needs the vocabulary touched:

  (a) The measured formation proof cone is the formation. It ends at the
      write-authority handoff D sealed. Teardown is the harness ending the
      scenario, is not formation, and is outside F's domain by scope. F4 can
      close on the formation cone.

  (b) The cone is the whole scenario. Then teardown is PRODUCTION_UNOWNED with
      no owner available, and the vocabulary question is open.

Reading (a) is the one I would argue for, because the live calibration measures
formation and a live run's process shutdown is outside its window too - but
that is the owner's call, not a classification I should make by choosing a
window that happens to zero a number.

F4: THE FROZEN FORMATION ATTRIBUTION PACKET.

THE WINDOW IS PRODUCTION'S WINDOW, and the correspondence is named rather than

THE LAST UNKNOWN WAS RESOLVED, NOT SCOPED AWAY. Moving the window did not
remove it: five frameless segments remained, four of them resources that
already existed when the window opened - the probe's own process startup and
the tail of module loading - and one promise created from an unframed parent
early in the window. Two things fixed it, and neither is a scope argument.
The census now lets the loop drain before it opens the window, so pre-existing
resources have dispatched; and a resource whose init the window never saw is
classified as pre_window_resource, which is a statement about causality - it
predates formation and carries no formation lineage - and needs no repository
frame, because a V8 promise continuation may not have one. unknown is 0, and
no unknownDetail row remains.

TWO KINDS OF REPAIR, and only one of them makes the table stale.

  Simulator-only correspondence repairs: restoring the StartupPipelineRunner
  entry, and carrying an AsyncResource across the virtual adapter timer. These
  do NOT invalidate the historical run. A real Node timer already creates its
  async resource when armed, so a live process never lost that lineage; the

  Production attribution-semantic repairs: the protocol task tracker's

Nothing is claimed about how much of the simulator's newly attributed Raft work
was unattributed in the old live run. The two arms were never measured under

FAIL CLOSED, at the narrowest existing mechanism. formation-seed-2026-09-13.json
carries its own supersession record and loadCalibration() refuses it with
calibration_superseded unless the caller states what it is reading it for. The
metered oracle states it: within-run determinism, never correspondence,
owner-rate ratios or coefficient selection. Any new consumer must make the same
statement in the same place, where a reviewer sees it - so the table cannot be
silently consumed as current coefficients. A witness proves the refusal, proves
the acknowledged read carries the supersession on the loaded object rather than
hiding it, and proves a manifest without the record loads without one. The
guard is about attribution semantics, not a commit: a later head may consume a
valid calibration unchanged.
